title: Decidability in Natural Numbers with a Combined Function
body: It is well known that there is no algorithm to determine whether a given first-order sentence is true in the structure of natural numbers with both addition and multiplication. In contrast, Presburger arithmetic , which involves natural numbers with addition but without multiplication, is decidable. Now, consider this function which combines addition and multiplication: $$ a \oplus b \mapsto (a + b)^2 $$ If we consider the structure of natural numbers with just this function, is there an algorithm that can determine whether a first-order sentence is true in this structure or not?

title: Counting words that agree at some place with each of their cyclic permutations
body: Let $a(m,n)$ be the number of words $W$ of length $m$ in an alphabet of $n$ letters, which have the property that each cyclic permutation of $W,$ has the same letter as $W$ in some place. For example, $aabcb$ counts (for $m=5$ and $n\ge 3$ ), since its cyclic permutations $baabc,$ $cbaab,$ $bcbaa,$ $abcba,$ agree with it at places 2, 5, 3, 1. But $aabbc$ does not count, because it disagrees with $bcaab$ everywhere. Some values of $a(m,n)$ for small $m$ are as follows: $a(1,n)=a(2,n)=n$ $a(3,n)=n(3n-2)$ $a(4,n)=n(4n-3)$ $a(5,n)=n+15n(n-1)^2$ $a(6,n)=n+3n(n-1)^2(4n+1)$ $a(7,n)=n+7n(n−1)(2n^3+5n^2−29n+31)$ $a(8,n)=n+4n(n−1)(24n^3−66n^2+37n+27)$ $a(9,n)=n+3n(n−1)(87n^4−369n^3+292n^2+811n−1145)$ The formulae for $m\ge 5$ are due to Fabius Wiesner (see comments). It thus appears that $a(m,n)$ is a polynomial in $n$ for each $m.$ (This is clear in fact - see below.) Is a general formula for $a(m,n)$ known? Incidental remark: When $m$ is prime, the action of the cyclic group of order $m$ on the set of counted words shows that $(a(m,n)-n)/m$ is an integer. When $m=5$ this ratio is $3n(n-1)^2,$ which is also the number of 2 x 2 planar subsets of a 3 x 3 cube (OEIS sequence A270205). This is probably a coincidence, but I mention it in case there is a nice reason. Based on Fabius Wiesner's notes (see comments below) it may be more enlightening to write $$a(m,n)=\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}b(m,r)\left(\begin{matrix}n\\r\end{matrix}\right)$$ where $b(m,r)=\sum_{s=1}^r(-1)^{r-s}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}r\\s\end{smallmatrix}\right)a(m,s)$ is the number of words with the given property, that use exactly all the first $r$ letters in the alphabet. The expression for $b(m,r)$ is the inclusion-exclusion formula. Then the formulae above become: $a(1,n)=a(2,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(3,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+6\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(4,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+8\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(5,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+30\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right) +90\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(6,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+54\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right) +306\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)+288\left(\begin{matrix}n\\4\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(7,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+126\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)+1428\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)+3864\left(\begin{matrix}n\\4\end{matrix}\right)+1680\left(\begin{matrix}n\\5\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(8,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+232\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)+3912\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)+14400\left(\begin{matrix}n\\4\end{matrix}\right)+11520\left(\begin{matrix}n\\5\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(9,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+510\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)+16470\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)+126432\left(\begin{matrix}n\\4\end{matrix}\right)+305640\left(\begin{matrix}n\\5\end{matrix}\right)+187920\left(\begin{matrix}n\\6\end{matrix}\right)$ $a(10,n)=\left(\begin{matrix}n\\1\end{matrix}\right)+990\left(\begin{matrix}n\\2\end{matrix}\right)+45630\left(\begin{matrix}n\\3\end{matrix}\right)+460200\left(\begin{matrix}n\\4\end{matrix}\right)+1506000\left(\begin{matrix}n\\5\end{matrix}\right)+1605600\left(\begin{matrix}n\\6\end{matrix}\right)+403200\left(\begin{matrix}n\\7\end{matrix}\right)$ This formulation makes it clear why $a(m,n)$ is a polynomial in $n,$ and shows that it would be enough to determine $b(m,r)$ for $1\le r<m.$ It would be interesting to know just the degree of the polynomial, i.e. to understand when $b(m,r)=0.$ See comments for some remarks on this question. Remark: Factorizing the $b(m,r)$ The group $C_m\times S_r$ acts on the words counted by $b(m,r).$ For $r>1,$ the orbits are mostly regular; this must hold when $m$ is prime, so that $b(m,r)$ is divisible by $m\cdot r!$ for $m$ prime and $r>1;$ for example $b(7,4)=3864=7\cdot 4!\cdot 23.$ But for example, $b(6,2)$ is not divisible by $12$ and $b(6,3)$ is not divisible by $36;$ the words $aabaab$ and $aabaac$ have nontrivial stabilizers in $C_6\times S_2$ and $C_6\times S_3$ respectively.

title: The definition and properties of the restriction of integral （rational） cohomology to a subspace within the ambient space.
body: This seems to be a fairly standard question, but I am somewhat confused when considering it using Čech cohomology theory. Let $X$ be a paracompact topological space admitting good cover and $Y$ a subspace of $X$ . Assume $\alpha\in H^p(X, \mathbb{Z})$ (or $\alpha\in H^p(X, \mathbb{Q})$ or or $\alpha\in H^p(X, \mathbb{R})$ ) be a cohomology class. ( $H^p(X, \mathbb{Z})$ denotes the sheaf cohomology of the locally constant sheaf $\mathbb{Z}$ , a priori.) Question : What is the definition of the restriction $\alpha|_Y$ to $Y$ , and is $\alpha|_Y\in H^p(Y, \mathbb{Z})$ ? I have seen from many references that $\alpha|_Y$ is well-defined and $\alpha|_Y\in H^p(Y, \mathbb{Z})$ . Now I will try to use Čech cohomology theory to define $\left.\alpha\right|_Y$ as follows. Since $X$ admits a good cover, we can choose a good cover $\left\{U_i\right\}_i$ (which is clearly an acyclic cover of $\mathbb{Z}$ ) and use the Leray isomorphism theorem. Then $\alpha$ can be represented by a p-cocycle $\left\{\alpha_{i_0\cdots i_p}\right\}$ with respect to $\left\{U_i\right\}_i$ . However, it may happen that $\left\{U_i \cap Y\right\}_i$ is not a good cover of $Y$ . Therefore, $\left\{\left.\alpha_{i_0\cdots i_p}\right|_Y\right\}$ may not represent an element of $H^p(Y, \mathbb{Z})$ .

title: Symmetric differentiation of real functions
body: Let a function $f:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ and $x\in \mathbb{R}$ . $f$ is symmetrically continuous in $x$ if $\lim\limits_{h\to 0} [f(x+h)-f(x-h)] = 0$ . $f$ is symmetrically differentiable in $x$ if $f'_s(x)=\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}$ exists finite. $f$ is symmetrically differentiable twice in $x$ if $f''_s(x)=\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2}$ exists finite. Now: $f$ twice differentiable --> $f$ differentiable --> $f$ continue (in classic sense) $\hspace{2cm} \downarrow$ $\hspace{5cm} \downarrow$ $\hspace{3cm} \downarrow$ $f$ twice sym.differentiable $\hspace{0.5cm}$ $f$ sym.differentiable --> $f$ sym.continue My question is: if twice symmetric differentiability implies symmetric differentiability? My attempt: Suppose $f''_s(x)$ exists finite. Then $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}=\dfrac{h}{2}\biggl[\dfrac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2}+\dfrac{ 2f(x) -2 f(x - h)}{h^2}\biggr]=\dfrac{h}{2}\biggl[\dfrac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2}\biggr]+\dfrac{ f(x) - f(x - h)}{h}\longrightarrow0\cdot f''_s(x)+\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\dfrac{ f(x) - f(x - h)}{h}$ And now?

title: Stanford Math Tournament Calculus Problem: Probability that a frog with uniformly distributed step length can pass an abyss on real line
body: A frog hops on the real number line, starting from the origin: Each second, it moves right uniformly at random a distance between $0$ and $1$ . There is an abyss between $1$ and $5/4$ , and if the frog lands there it will fall into the abyss. If the frog makes it to or passes $3$ without falling in the abyss, then the frog is safe. $$ \large\mbox{What is the probability it is safe ?.} $$ Let us invoke Irwin Hall Distribution and work on the probability of falling into abyss and then inferring probability that it is safe. The CDF of the sum of $n$ independent random variables uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$ [ 1 ]: $$P(X\le x,n) = \dfrac{1}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor x \rfloor} (-1)^k {n\choose k} {(x-k)}^n$$ Thus $P(X\le x)$ , given that x of abyss is in the range $(1\le x \le2)$ , for n=1, $P(X\le x) =1$ for n=2, $P(X\le x) = \dfrac{1}{2.2!}\left[(-1)^0.{2\choose0}x^2 +(-1)^1.{2\choose 1} (x-1)^2\right]$ For n=3, $P(X\le x) =\dfrac{1}{3.3!}\left[ (-1)^0.{3\choose0}x^3 +(-1)^1.{3\choose 1} (x-1)^3\right]$ and n=.. To summarise CDF can be be written such as $P(X\le x) = \left[1+ \dfrac{x^2}{2.2!}+\dfrac{x^3}{3.3!}+\cdots\right] - \left[ \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2!} + \dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3!}-\cdots\right]$ PDF is the derivative of this P(X = x) $= \left[\dfrac{(x)}{2!}+\dfrac{(x^2)}{3!}+\cdots \right] - \left[(x-1) + \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2!}+\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3!}+\cdots\right]$ This translates $ P(X= x) = \dfrac{(e^x - 1)}{x} - e^{x-1}$ Thus $P(\text{falling into the abyss}) = \int_{1}^{5/4} P(X=x) = 0.178761$ $P(\text{the frog is safe}) = 1-.178761 = 0.821$ It sounds logical but to see if abyss happens to be (1.1 and 1.75),say, the probability results in 0.56 https://www.stanfordmathtournament.com/pdfs/smt2023/calculus-tiebreaker-solutions.pdf

title: Could we approximate $\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^4}dx$ using a Riemann sum?
body: We know that in one dimension, the integral $\int_{0}^{1}\left(1/x^{4}\right){\rm d}x$ is not finite. But could we approximate this integral using a Riemann Sum ?. In particular, if we divide the interval $\left[0,1\right]$ into equal-length partitions $$ 0 = x_{0} \leq x_{1} \leq \cdots \leq x_{n} = 1\quad \mbox{with}\quad \Delta_{i} = \left\vert x_{i}-x_{i-1}\right\vert = \frac{1}{n}\,\,\, \forall\ 1\leq i\leq n $$ Do we have $\sum_{i=1}^n \Delta_if(x_{i})$ converge to $\int_{1/n}^{1}\left(1/x^{4}\right){\rm d}x$ as $n\to \infty\ ?$ . Could we give a bound on the difference $$ \left\vert\int_{1/n}^{1}\frac{1}{x^{4}}\,{\rm d}x - \sum_{k = 1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left(k/n\right)^{4}}\frac{1}{n}\right\vert $$ to get the rate of convergence of the Riemann sum as $n\to \infty$ ?. title: Bound for norm of projection onto $k$-dimensional subspace in terms of projections onto basis vectors
body: Let $V$ a finite-dimensional vector space with inner product $\langle, \rangle$ . Let $v_1,\dots,v_k \in V$ linearly independent vectors of unit length. Let $p_i:V \rightarrow \text{span}(v_i)$ defined by $p_i(w):=\langle v_i,w \rangle v_i$ be the projection onto the one-dimensional subspace spanned by $v_i$ for $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$ . Let $p:V \rightarrow \text{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $k$ -dimensional subspace spanned by $v_1,\dots,v_k$ . Question: is there an upper bound for $|p(w)|$ in terms of $p_i(w)$ and products/volumes computed involving $v_1,\dots,v_k$ ? Here, $|\cdot |=\sqrt{\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle}$ . If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are pairwise orthonormal, then $|p(w)|^2=\sum_{i=1}^k |p_i(w)|^2$ . In the case of $k=2$ and $v_1,v_2$ having unit length (but not necessarily being orthogonal), I would expect something like $|p(w)| \leq \frac{1}{1+\langle v_1,v_2 \rangle}(|p_1(w)|+|p_2(w)|)$ to hold, but I wasn't able to show that. (The fraction can attain a large value if $\langle v_1,v_2 \rangle$ is close to $-1$ , but by the assumption that $v_1,v_2$ be linearly dependent, it is always well defined.) If $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ and $A=(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ denotes the matrix consisting of the column vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ written next to each other, then $p=AA^+$ , where $A^+$ denotes the pseudo-inverse of $A$ . If one could get an upper bound for the norm of $A^+ w$ in terms of $p_i(w)$ and products/volumes computed involving $v_1,\dots,v_k$ , that would solve the problem, but I don't know if that's possible.

title: Question about the proof of Hartshorne II, Prop 5.12
body: This is a follow up of the question Here . Let me redescribe the context below: Let $\varphi:S\rightarrow T$ be a morphism of graded rings. Let $M$ be a graded $S$ -module and $N$ be a graded $T$ -module. Let $f:U\rightarrow Proj(S)$ denote the induced morphism of schemes, where $U=\{P\in \operatorname{Proj}(T) : \varphi(S_+)\not\subset P\}$ . We have a canonical morphism $$ \Psi\colon f^\ast(\widetilde{M})\to (M\otimes_S T)^{\sim}\vert_{U}. $$ and $$ \Phi\colon f_\ast(\widetilde{N}|_U)\to ({}_{S} N)^{\sim}. $$ In Hartshorne's statements, he added the assumption that $T$ is generated by $T_1$ as a $T_0$ -algebra and $S$ is generated by $S_1$ as a $S_0$ -algebra. Basically to check the above two were isomorphism, it suffice to check on the affine opens, specifically I mean the sets $D_+(f)$ , where $f\in S_1$ . One were able to show that $$ f^\ast(\widetilde{M})|_{D_+(\varphi(f))}=(M_{(f)}\otimes_{S_{(f)}} T_{(\varphi(f))})^{\sim} \cong (M\otimes_S T)^{\sim}\vert_{D_+(\varphi(f))} $$ and similarly $$ f_\ast(\widetilde{N}|_{D_+(\varphi(f))} )= f_\ast((N_{(\varphi(f))})^\sim ) \cong ({ }_{S_{(f)}} N_{(\varphi(f))})^\sim \cong ({ }_{S_{(f)}} N_{(f)})^\sim \cong ({ }_S N)^\sim|_{D(f)} $$ Again, Hartshorne writes that, under the assumption that $T$ is generated by $T_1$ as a $T_0$ -algebra and $S$ is generated by $S_1$ as a $S_0$ -algebra, this map is an isomorphism. But the above isomorphisms does not seem to use the assumptions on $T$ at all. I was wondering if the assumptions for $T_1$ not being finitely generated over $T_0$ by $T_1$ in both cases could be lifted. Any helps would be appreciated.

title: Can we relax the assumptions and still get a.s. convergence?
body: Assume you have a sequence of independent Bernoulli random variables $X_i$ each with probability $p_i$ . Let $c_i$ be a sequence of real numbers and $ m$ be a real numbers such that $c_1>0$ and with $0 \le m <c_i< \infty $ . Define $$Y_n=\frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i X_i -\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i p_i}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i}.$$ Then $Y_n$ converges a.s to zero. (Proof below). Questions: Is my proof correct? Does the result also hold with $m= 0$ ? Proof: Define $$Z_i = c_i (X_i-p_i).$$ Then $E[z_i]=0$ . By the strong law of large numbers we have that $\bar{Z_n} \rightarrow 0$ a.s. We also have $\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i > m\cdot n$ , so we have $n< \sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i/m$ . Hence we have $$|Y_n| =\left| \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n Z_i }{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i }\right| =\frac{n}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n c_i }\cdot |\bar{Z_n}|<\frac{1}{m}\cdot |\bar{Z_n}| ,$$ and the last quantity goes to zero a.s.

title: How many definite elementary integrals can be substituted between?
body: There are three types of definite integrals that I can think of. Those that equal $0$ , those that equal $A\neq0$ and those that diverge through some manner. If $$\int\limits_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=A\neq0$$ then we can form its normalised integral $$\frac{1}{A}\int\limits_{a}^{b}f(x)dx=1$$ Some examples would be something like $$1=\int\limits_{0}^{1}dx\\ =\frac{1}{\ln(4)}\int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\operatorname{sgn}(x)-\tanh(x)|dx\\ =\int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sec^{2}(x)dx\\ =\frac{2}{\pi}\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\operatorname{sinc}(x)\operatorname{sinc}(\frac{x}{3})\operatorname{sinc}(\frac{x}{5})dx$$ Given that these are all equal (because we're taking the normalised integrals) can we make explicit substitutions between them, to get from one to the other? The constants are just there for equality to hold, the meat is in the actual form of the integrand. It's a similar story for those equalling $0$ . $$0=\int\limits_{1}^{1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}dx\\ =\int\limits_{2}^{4}0dx\\ =\int\limits_{0}^{2\lceil{|z|}\rceil\pi}\sin(x)dx$$ These are equal, so can we manipulate substitutions to go from one to the other? My initial guess for both is no. If we had an integrand with a non-elementary antiderivative, like $\ln(\sec(x))$ , then it couldn't be related to $x$ because then there'd be a chain of elementary functions leading to it, giving it an elementary antiderivative. Still, could all equal integrals with elementary antiderivatives be subbed between, and all those that also involve $\operatorname{erf(x)}$ be subbed between, and all those with both $\operatorname{Li}(x)$ and $\operatorname{Li}_{2}(x)$ , and so on?

title: Are there terminologies for "one-to-one" but not "onto" functions, and "onto" but not "one-to-one" functions?

title: If a graded ring $S$ is a UFD, then $S_0$ is a UFD
body: Let $S$ be a commutative graded ring ( $S = \oplus_{n \in Z} S_n$ ). If $S$ is a UFD, can we deduce $S_0$ is a UFD? I think $S_0$ is a UFD. Because we can gather all the finite product of the irreducible elements in $S_0$ , that is $$ \{p_{1} p_{2} \dots p_m \in S_0 | p_1, \dots, p_m \mbox{ are irreducible in } S\}, $$ Then $S_0$ has enough irreducible elements to represent all the elements as products of $S_0$ . The problem comes from Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry (II, 6.17), where we need to verify the degree- $0$ ring of every localization of $k[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is a UFD.

title: First order ode with tricky BC at infinity.
body: This is problem 94, page 41 from book "A book of problems in ordinary differential equations" by Krasnov,Kiselyov, Makarenko (very hard to find book, so no PDF online, and paper copies are very expensive) In Latex \begin{align*} x^{3} y'-\sin \left(y \right) &= 1\\ y(\infty) &= 5\pi \end{align*} General solution is easy to find as it is separable. So just integration. But I am not able to get the final solution for the BC given. Could someone see what is wrong with my solution? Back of the book, page 301, authors give answer as $$ y = 2 \arctan\left( 1- \frac{1}{2 x^2} \right) + \frac{9}{2}\pi $$ I verified the book solution using the computer to be correct. Here is my solution. Solve \begin{align*} x^{3}y^{\prime}-\sin y & =1\\ y\left( \infty\right) & =5\pi \end{align*} Writing the ode as $$ y^{\prime}=\frac{1+\sin y}{x^{3}}\qquad x\neq0 $$ Shows it is separable $$ \frac{dy}{1+\sin y}=\frac{dx}{x^{3}} $$ Integrating gives \begin{align*} \int\frac{dy}{1+\sin y} & =\int\frac{dx}{x^{3}}\\ \frac{-2}{\tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) +1} & =-\frac{1}{2x^{2}}+c\\ \frac{2}{\tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) +1} & =\frac{1}{2x^{2}}-c\\ \frac{2}{\tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) +1} & =\frac{1-2x^{2}c}{2x^{2}}\\ \tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) +1 & =\frac{4x^{2}}{1-2x^{2}c}\\ \tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) & =\frac{4x^{2}}{1-2x^{2}c}-1\\ \tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) & =\frac{4x^{2}-\left( 1-2x^{2}c\right) }{1-2x^{2}c}\\ \tan\left( \frac{y}{2}\right) & =\frac{4x^{2}-1+2x^{2}c}{1-2x^{2}c}% \end{align*} Hence \begin{align} \frac{y}{2} & =\arctan\left( \frac{4x^{2}-1+2x^{2}c}{1-2x^{2}c}\right) +\pi n\qquad n\in %TCIMACRO{\U{2124} } \mathbb{Z} \nonumber\\ y & =2\left( \arctan\left( \frac{4x^{2}-1+2x^{2}c}{1-2x^{2}c}\right) +\pi n\right) \tag{1} \end{align} Applying IC gives, and taking limit $\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}\left( \frac{4x^{2}-1+2x^{2}c}{1-2x^{2}c}\right) =-\frac{4+2c}{2c}$ then the above becomes \begin{align*} 5\pi & =2\left( \arctan\left( -\frac{4+2c}{2c}\right) +\pi n\right) \\ & =2\arctan\left( -\frac{4+2c}{2c}\right) +2\pi n\\ \frac{5\pi-2\pi n}{2} & =\arctan\left( -\frac{4+2c}{2c}\right) \\ \frac{2\pi n-5\pi}{2} & =\arctan\left( \frac{4+2c}{2c}\right) \end{align*} The range of $\arctan$ is $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ . Hence we need $\frac{2\pi n-5\pi}{2}$ to be in this range. This means $2\pi n-5\pi$ should be between $-\pi\cdots\pi$ but not including the edge points. Value of $n$ which allows this is $n=-\frac{5}{2}$ . (but $n$ should be an integer. There is no integer solution. What to do?) But if we continue, then we have \begin{align*} \arctan\left( \frac{4+2c}{2c}\right) & =0\qquad n=-\frac{5}{2}\\ 4+2c & =0\\ c & =-2 \end{align*} Hence the solution in (1) becomes \begin{align*} y & =2\left( \arctan\left( \frac{4x^{2}-1+2x^{2}c}{1-2x^{2}c}\right) -\frac{5}{2}\pi\right) \\ & =2\arctan\left( \frac{-1}{1+4x^{2}}\right) -5\pi\\ & =-2\arctan\left( \frac{1}{1+4x^{2}}\right) -5\pi \end{align*} But this solution does not satisfy the ode. Btw, neither Maple nor Mathematica are able to solve this ode !

title: Sangaku problem involving eight circles
body: I made the following sangaku problem. $\dfrac{\text{Area of the orange circle}}{\text{Area of a blue circle}}=\space ?$ Description of diagram . In this question, circles of the same color are congruent. A chain of five tangent blue circles lies on top of a larger orange circle, such that each circle in the chain is tangent to the orange circle. Another blue circle sits on top of the chain's middle circle. A black circle encloses all of the orange and blue circles, such that the black circle is tangent to the orange circle, the left and right circles in the chain, and the circle on top of the chain. I used a computer to work out that the answer is: 5 but I would like to know how to do this without a computer. My attempt Assume the blue circles have radius $1$ and the orange circle radius has $r$ , where $r$ is a constant to be found. Superimpose a cartesian coordinate system with the origin at the orange circle's centre. The black circle has equation $$x^2+(y-2)^2=(r+2)^2\tag1$$ The rightmost circle in the chain has equation $$\left(x-(r+1)\sin\left(4\arcsin\frac{1}{r+1}\right)\right)^2+\left(y-(r+1)\cos\left(4\arcsin\frac{1}{r+1}\right)\right)^2=1\tag2$$ In $(2)$ we can use the compound angle formulas $\cos(4\arcsin\alpha)=8\alpha^4-8\alpha^2+1$ and $\sin(4\arcsin\alpha)=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}(4\alpha-8\alpha^3)$ . We want to find $r$ such that $(1)$ and $(2)$ together has exactly one solution. $(1)-(2)$ yields an equation that can be rearranged to get $y=f(x)$ , which can be put into $(1)$ to get a quadratic in $x$ . Then set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $r$ . Then the answer to the OP is $r^2$ . But this approach is very difficult without a computer. Fun facts Two more blue circles fit perfectly in the spaces above the chain's second-from-end circles (I asked about this in a Geometry question about a six-pack of beer ). And there are many sets of collinear points, as shown. Edit As shown in the Fun Fact diagram, an extended horizontal diameter of the orange circle is tangent to the bottom two blue circles. Here I will explain why this is true, in order to support @Edward Porcella's answer . Start with a closed chain of ten tangent congruent blue circles, all internally tangent to a black circle, with one of the blue circles touching the top point of the black circle. Draw a horizontal diameter of the black circle (which must be tangent to four blue circles). Draw an orange circle inside the black circle, touching all the blue circles. Remove the bottom five blue circles. Move the top five blue circles, and the orange circle, down, by a distance equal to the diameter of a blue circle. Add a blue circle at the top. This is the diagram in the OP, showing an extended horizontal diameter of the orange circle, which is tangent to the bottom two blue circles. Context I have been asking questions about circles here on MSE, and also on Mathematics Educators and Puzzling .

title: How to do Literal Equation $ax-bc=xb-ac$?
body: So I am doing year 9 maths, in an extension question which was about literal equations, I was stumped. It wanted me to find $x$ , using factorisation Here is the question: $$ax-bc = xb-ac$$ Here is how far I got before being lost. \begin{align*}ax-bc &= xb-ac\\ ax &= xb-ac+bc\\ ax &= xb+c(-a+b)\\ ax-bx &= c(-a+b)\\ x(a-b) &= c(a-b)\\ x &= c(a-b)/a-b\\ x &= c,\end{align*} but my textbook says that the answer is actually $-c$ . I am having trouble seeing how they get that. Please explain if you can. I cant add an image but here is what it says Short Solution Steps $c(-a+b)/(a-b)$ Factor the expressions that are not already factored. $c(-a+b)/(a-b)$ Extract the negative sign in $-a+b$ . $-с(а-b)/(a-b)$ Cancel out $a-b$ in both numerator and denominator. $-c$ Just for confirmation. title: Why is the material conditional treated like logical entailment in second order quantification?
body: According to this Wikipedia article the second order axiom of induction is: $$\forall P(P(0)\land \forall k(P(k) \to P(k+1)) \to \forall x(N(x) \to P(x))$$ Where N(x) means x is a natural number. That x is a natural was implied in the article so I added it into the axiom to make it explicit. This axiom is also given informally along with the rest of the Peano axioms here. Now what the Wikipedia article for Peano arithmetic claims is that "The intuitive notion that each natural number can be obtained by applying successor sufficiently many times to zero requires an additional axiom, which is sometimes called the axiom of induction." However, this claim appeared at first to me to be false. My reasoning went like this. The material conditional $\to$ does not mean that what is to the left of it logically entails what is to the right of it. For instance $A \to B$ does not mean "A logically entails B." In a logical proof $A \to B$ is a premise precisely because it is not logically self-evident. Likewise, $P(0)\land \forall k(P(k) \to P(k+1))$ may imply that $\forall x(N(x) \to P(x))$ in terms of truth tables, but this does not mean that the first statement logically entails the second. This means that non-standard models may still exist as long as the first statement is false or the second statement is true, since $A \to B \equiv \lnot A \lor B$ . Consider the case where the property P is true for all of the standard natural numbers (so the antecedent is true) and P is also true for all standard natural numbers as well as some non-standard natural numbers in N (the consequent is true). Every P that applies to all standard natural numbers may also apply for all non-standard natural numbers. Then the axiom is affirmed for all P and yet there remain non-standard models. I suspect what is happening here is that in second order logic, P(a) is interpreted to mean $\exists x \phi$ $(x:=a)$ , where $\exists x \phi$ is the "sentence", of which a is the "subject" and everything stated about a in the formula is the "predicate" P. Assuming this, $\forall P$ is interpreted to mean "for all possible formulas $\phi$ , when a, b, ... is substituted into them, the following formula $\psi$ is true, if P(a), P(b) ... denotes $\exists x \phi$ $(x:=a)$ , $\exists x \phi$ $(x:=b)$ " In this case second order quantification is quantifying over all possible formulas that could be applied to some variable(s). Of course with the caveat that these theoretical formulas could be infinitely long, whereas written formulas can only be finite. In this case the axiom of induction is stating that every possible formula for which the antecedent is true implies the consequent is true. Since every possible formula would include every possible truth assignment for natural numbers as well as non-standard natural numbers, then it includes the formula whose truth assignment is only true of the standard natural numbers. Importantly, it is assumed that all possible P includes the P which applies only to the standard model. If all P in "the set of all possible P" could have the same truth assignments, then it would be the same as first-order logic in terms of expressiveness. Is this basically correct?

title: How is it that Archimedes's spiral is the derivative of the unit circle w.r.t. $i$?
body: The unit circle in the complex plane is given by $z=e^{i\theta}$ . Therefore, $$ \frac{\partial z}{\partial i}=\theta e^{i\theta} $$ which is precisely Archimedes's spiral. This may be a fluke, but let's take it a step further. The Weyl Fractional Derivative formula for the exponential function is given by $$ _{-\infty}W_x^\alpha e^{ax}=a^\alpha e^{ax} $$ If we allow that that $x=i$ and $a=\theta$ , then we have that the fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ (positive or negative) gives the complete spectrum of Archimedean spirals, to wit, $$ D^\alpha e^{i\theta}=\theta^\alpha e^{i\theta} $$ For example, Fermat ( $\alpha=1/2$ ), Lituus ( $\alpha=-1/2$ ), and Hyperbolic ( $\alpha=-1$ ). The concept of differentiation with respect to $i$ is not a commonly used operation in mathematical or practical applications. But it is not unheard of either. So the question is, what, if anything, is the meaning of the (fractional) derivative with respect to $i$ ? Is it real (no pun intended) or all just all a coincidence?

title: Divergent Tail Sums of Approximations of Non-trace Class Compact Operators
body: I'm working on approximations of compact operators that are not trace class, and I'm looking for ways to provide meaningful approximation error estimates for truncated eigenfunction expansions. I understand that the error is bounded by the first omitted eigenvalue, even for non-trace class operators. However, I would like to obtain a tighter bound if possible. Here are a few concepts I'm considering: Cesàro Summation : Can Cesàro summation be used to assign a value to the divergent series of eigenvalues and provide a meaningful error bound? For a sequence $a_n$ , the Cesàro sum is defined as: $$ \sigma_N = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N S_k = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \sum_{n=1}^k a_n, $$ and the series is Cesàro summable to $\sigma$ if $\sigma_N$ tends to $\sigma$ as $N$ tends to infinity. Martingale Properties : If the sequence of partial sums $S_N$ forms a martingale, does the Martingale Convergence Theorem imply that Cesàro means should converge to a finite value, thus providing a stable error estimate? Ergodic Properties of Gaussian Processes : For ergodic Gaussian processes, time averages converge to ensemble averages. This is analogous to the Cesàro mean: $$ \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T X(t) \, dt, $$ where $X(t)$ is a sample path of the Gaussian process. Can these properties be used to handle divergent series and provide meaningful error bounds? Gaussian Inequalities : Inequalities such as the Borell-TIS inequality or Slepian's inequality provide bounds on the behavior of Gaussian processes. Can these inequalities help derive bounds on the Cesàro means or ensure that the averaging process yields a meaningful limit? Even for non-trace class operators, the bound provided by the first omitted eigenvalue still applies. However, I would like to calculate the tail sum if possible, as it would provide the actual error. Given these concepts, are there standard methods or theorems that can be used to provide a meaningful approximation error for truncating the approximations of compact operators that are not trace class? Any insights or references would be greatly appreciated.

title: Covariances not below $\Sigma$
body: $\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1,\dots,\Sigma_K$ are real covariance matrices. I’m interested in the set of matrices $$\bigcap_{k=1}^K \left\{x: 0 \preceq x \preceq \Sigma_0, \ x\not\prec\Sigma_k\right\}.$$ I’m looking for a concrete description of this set or of its convex hull. I haven’t been able to work one out from this definition. Can anyone provide clues? Superficially restated, a generic member $x$ has the following properties: $x$ is positive-semifefinite $\Sigma_0-x$ is positive-semidefinite $\Sigma_k-x$ is not positive-definite for $k=1,\dots,K$ . Here's a start, working in dimension $D$ . Write $(v_{k,d}, \sigma_{k,d}^2) \in \mathbb{R}^D \times \mathbb{R}$ as $\Sigma_k$ 's $d$ -th singular vector and value. Call each set in that intersection $S_k$ and $S=\cap_{k=1}^K S_k.$ Now $S_k$ is precisely those covariances $x \preceq \Sigma_0$ where $ v_{k,d}' x v_{k,d} \geq \sigma_{k,d}^2 \text{ for some } d \in [D]$ . That is, $S_k= \cup_{d=1}^D \{x: 0\preceq x \preceq \Sigma_0, \ v_{k,d}'x v_{k,d} \geq \sigma_{k,d}^2 \}$ , thus \begin{equation} S = \bigcup_{(d_1, \dots, d_K)} \left\{ x: 0 \preceq x \preceq \Sigma_0, \ v'_{k,d_k}xv_{k,d_k} \geq \sigma^2_{k,d_k},k=1,\dots,K \right\} \end{equation} where the union is taken over all $(d_1,\dots,d_K) \in [D]^K.$ Further questions remain: Is this correct? The number of union members explodes with $K$ and I think many of those members are redundant. Is there a more convenient representation or approximation to this set? For example, starting from $(\Sigma_k)_{k=0}^K$ is there a fast algorithm to find some covariances $(C_n)_n$ whose convex hull contains $S$ ?

title: Schur’s lemma over $\mathbb{F}_p$
body: I’m studying modular representation theory, and I got really stuck with the seemingly innocent statement. Consider $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ and its center $Z$ , which is just a set of all scalar matrices. Now let $\pi: \mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) \to \mathrm{GL}(V) $ be an irreducible representation over $\mathbb{F}_p$ . Show that any $z\in Z$ is also a scalar operator in representation ( $\pi(z) = \alpha\cdot \mathsf{Id}_{V}$ for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_p$ ). And for algebraically closed field this is a one liner, as by commutative nature of $z$ we know that $\pi(z)$ is an endmorphism of $(\pi,V)$ , for which Schur’s Lemma states exactly that it is scalar. However this doesn’t work for $\mathbb{F}_p$ , as not all endimorohisms of $V$ have eigenvalues. We can generalize Schur’s Lemma and say that if we have a finite group $G$ and it’s irreducible representation $(\pi,V)$ , then we know that $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{F}_p[G]}(V)$ is a division ring. Since we’re over a finite field, $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{F}_p[G]}(V)$ is also a field, but I am not sure that it is exactly $\mathbb{F}_p$ , why couldn’t it be a field $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$ ? And I’m also interested what is the best Schur’s Lemma adaptation for a finite field case.

title: Question about Deformation Retractions in Fomenko and Fuchs
body: Working through Anatoly Fomenko and Dmitry Fuchs' "Homotopical Topology". As an offhand comment, they mention: $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$ if and only if the inclusion map $A \rightarrow X$ is a homotopy equivalence. Here are the definitions we're using: a retract is a continuous map $X \rightarrow A \subseteq X$ , which fixes every point in $A$ . A deformation retract is a retract that is homotopic to the identity on $X$ (the homotopy does not necessarily need to fix every point in $A$ ; if it does, they call that a strong deformation retract). Here's the textbook phrasing: "If a retraction $r : X \rightarrow X$ of X onto A is homotopic to the identity id $_X : X \rightarrow X$ , then $A$ is called a deformation retract of $X$ ." The definition of homotopy equivalence is the standard one (maps which are inverses up to homotopy). One direction is easy; clearly if there's a deformation retract, then it forms a homotopy inverse for the inclusion. I found myself surprisingly stuck in the reverse direction, though. If the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, there's still no guarantee that the homotopy inverse has to be a retract (IE, no guarantee that its inverse has to fix points in $A$ ). For an explicit counterexample (not to the problem as a whole, but to the idea that the homotopy inverse of the inclusion must be a retract), consider the map $f : B_{1}(0) \subseteq \mathbb{C} \rightarrow B_{\frac{1}{2}}(0)$ given by $re^{i\theta} \mapsto \frac{r}{2}e^{i(\theta + \frac{\pi}{2})}$ . Clearly this forms a homotopy inverse for the inclusion in the other direction, but it's also definitely not a retract. Of course, in this case there's a much simpler homotopy inverse which is a retract, but I'm finding it hard to convince myself that this must be true in general, even for pathological topological spaces.

title: From quenched to annealed limit theorems

For $3x+y\equiv 2\pmod {10}$ , the congruences are $3x\equiv 2\pmod {1}$ and $y\equiv 3\pmod {3}$ . I would say that this doesn't help. title: How to maximize $\mathbf{E}(XY) $ if we know the distribution of $X$ and $Y$
body: Given two discrete random variables (X) and (Y) with known distributions. The contingency table is provided: \begin{array}{c|ccc|c} & Y=1 & Y=2 & Y=3 & \text{Total} \\ \hline X=1 & a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} & \mathbf{P}(X=1) = \frac{1}{2} \\ X=2 & a_{21} & a_{22} & a_{23} & \mathbf{P}(X=2) = \frac{1}{4} \\ X=3 & a_{31} & a_{32} & a_{33} & \mathbf{P}(X=3) = \frac{1}{4} \\ \hline \text{Total} & \mathbf{P}(Y=1) = \frac{1}{3} & \mathbf{P}(Y=2) = \frac{1}{3} & \mathbf{P}(Y=3) = \frac{1}{3} & 1 \end{array} We want to maximize $\mathbf{E}(XY) $ . We have: $\mathbf{E}(XY) = \sum_{i=1}^{3} \sum_{j=1}^{3} i \cdot j \cdot a_{ij} = a_{11} + 2a_{12} + 3a_{13} + 2a_{21} + 4a_{22} + 6a_{23} + 3a_{31} + 6a_{32} + 9a_{33}$ My idea is to maximize: $a_{11} + 2a_{12} + 3a_{13} + 2a_{21} + 4a_{22} + 6a_{23} + 3a_{31} + 6a_{32} + 9a_{33}$ subject to the constraints: \begin{align*} a_{11} + a_{12} + a_{13} &= \frac{1}{2} \\ a_{21} + a_{22} + a_{23} &= \frac{1}{4} \\ a_{31} + a_{32} + a_{33} &= \frac{1}{4} \\ a_{11} + a_{21} + a_{31} &= \frac{1}{3} \\ a_{12} + a_{22} + a_{32} &= \frac{1}{3} \\ a_{13} + a_{23} + a_{33} &= \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 \leq a_{ij} &\leq 1 \quad \forall i, j \end{align*} I wonder if this approach is correct and if there is a simpler way.

title: Revisit: A fair die is rolled until 3 (consecutive) 4's appear: what is the expected # of 2's and 3's?

body: I am conducting academic research on steerable needles with multiple sections and I have run into a roadblock. However, I am having trouble deriving how to find the rotation angle that I mentioned earlier. title: Investigate whether $f_n (x)=\frac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}$ on $[0,\infty),n\in \mathbb N$ converges uniformly or not.
body: Investigate whether $f_n (x)=\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}$ on $[0,\infty),n\in \mathbb N$ converges uniformly or not. Obviously, $f_n(x)$ pointwise converges to $0$ . Since $f_n(0)=0$ when $x=0$ and $\displaystyle\lim_ {n\to \infty} f_n(x)=\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}=0$ for $x \in (0,\infty)$ . Therefore $f_n(x)$ can converge uniformly to $0$ . To show that it indeed converges to $0$ , we need to check the following. $M_n=\displaystyle\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)} |f_n(x)-f(x)|\to 0$ . It turns out that $M_n=\displaystyle\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}-0\right|=\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}\right|$ . I want to play with inequalities so as to do I checked first derivative of $\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}$ which gives when function takes its maximum but I couldn't obtain something useful. After that I tried the following simply however I couldn't get rid of the term $x$ . $\begin{align}M_n&=\displaystyle\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}-0\right|=\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{nx}{1+n^3x^3}\right|\leqslant\\[3pt]&\leqslant\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{nx}{n^3x^3}\right|=\sup_{x\in [0,\infty)}\left|\dfrac{1}{n^2x^2}\right|.\end{align}$ Thanks in advance.

title: How can one intuitively understand the dependence of the set relative to which homotopies are constructed?
body: In the notes I am using, homotopy is defined relative to a set. To start the discussion I present the definition: Two functions $f,g:(X, \tau_x) \to (Y,\tau_y)$ are said to be homotopic relative to a set $\color{red}{A} \subset X$ , if there exists a continous function $H:X \times [0,1] \to Y$ which satisfies the following four properties: H is continous $H(x,0)=f(x)$ $H(x,1) = g(x)$ $\color{red}{H(a,\lambda) = f(a) = g(a)}$ How do I understand how homotopy changes as I change $A$ ? What I found so far: Obviously, if we make $A=X$ , then each function is only homotopic to itself. In the very simple case of functions between $\mathbb{R}$ , we have that if we choose $A$ to be empty, then all continous functions are homotopic to each other by the homotopy given by: $$H(x,\lambda) = f(x) + (g(x)-f(x)) \lambda$$ Which gives me a feeling that if we reduce the size of $A$ , more functions in $C(X,Y)$ are homotopic to each other.

title: Paper by Dmitriev and Dynkin on 'pre-Karpeleciv's' bound
body: There is a relatively well-known paper by N. Dmitriev and E. A year before, Dmitriev and Dynkin published a short paper on the same topic [3]. This earlier paper is rather obscure, and I have been unable to locate it. However, it seems to contain some important statements, specifically regarding the relationship between generators and stochastic matrices, which are not present in their 1946 publication. Does anyone have access to this paper? If so, could you share it with me? Alternatively, could you direct me to a source where I might find it? A brief history of my quest for the paper: It is mentioned in a paper [4] and a presentation [5] by Ádám Besenyei [6]. In the latter, he even references some results from [3]. I tried to contact him using two email addresses I found, but both emails were returned with "could not be delivered because the email does not exist." Today I discovered that Besenyei passed away in December 2022 [7]. In his paper [4], Besenyei thanks "Craig Smoryński for sending a copy of the paper" (which is the paper by Dmitriev and Dynkin in question). Smoryński has published numerous books on various mathematical topics, but it seems he retired quite a while ago, and it is unclear if he is still alive. [1] N. Dmitriev, E. title: What are some applications of homotopy in topology other than constructing fundamental group (and higher homotopy groups)??
body: In pretty much all books I've seen, homotopy is introduced for the pure purposes of defining the fundamental group. But, what are some other of uses of homotopy? One that I found is that it can be used to characterize path connectedness; Two functions from a given topological space to the space with only a point (and of course, obvious topology) is homotopic, iff all functions between these two spaces are homotopic relative to the empty set. Furthermore, we can check if a space has holes (in a very geometric sense) by checking if a map of circle into a space is homotopic to a constant function relative to a single point on the circle. I am also aware of the application in complex analysis where the complex line integral between two points can be shown to have the same value on paths upto homotopy.

title: Converse of Intermediate Value Theorem via Nonstandard Analysis
body: I am working through Goldblatt's Lectures on the Hyperreals , and I am stuck on Exercise 7.8.4 (p. 82). It is a converse to the Intermediate Value Theorem: "Let the real function $f$ be monotonic on $[a,b]$ , and suppose that for all real $r$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ there exists a real $c\in[a,b]$ such that $f(c)=r$ . Prove that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ ." Standard proofs are abundant. I am specifically looking for a proof using nonstandard analysis. For instance, for continuity I am anticipating that I will have to show that for every $c\in[a,b]$ and for every (hyperreal) $x\in{}^*\mathbb{R}$ such that $x\simeq c$ , we have $f(x)\simeq f(c)$ . The notation $a\simeq b$ means that $a$ is "infinitely close" to $b$ , meaning $a-b$ is infinitesimal. For the most part, Goldblatt exercises are short and sweet, but this one is completely evading me. I've tried many things (both direct and by contradiction) but can't possibly include them all here. I can't seem to formulate a helpful statement to use transfer on. Say I start with $x\simeq c$ . If $x=c$ , then of course $f(x)\simeq f(c)$ . So let's try the case $x>c$ . By transferring monotonicity (assuming, say, nondecreasing), we should have $f(x)\ge f(c)$ . If $f(x)=f(c)$ , we are again done, so let's assume $f(x)>f(c)$ . So at this point we could take an arbitrary $f(x)>y>f(c)$ . By transferring the IVT property, we would get some $x'\in{}^*\mathbb{R}$ such that $c<x'<x$ and $y=f(x')$ . This would imply that $x'\simeq c$ , but I'm not sure what more this says. I could take a sequence of $y$ 's that get closer to $f(c)$ , but I'm not sure how that would imply the original $f(x)$ is infinitely close to $f(c)$ . This is starting to feel like a standard proof anyway.

title: A category has local initial objects if and only if it has a coreflective subgroupoid
body: Given a category $C$ , say that $C$ has local initial objects if every slice category of $C$ has an initial object. In category theory, there are two different meanings of "locally": one applying to Hom-sets, and the other to slice categories. The former applies to "locally small", while the latter applies to "locally cartesian closed". The latter meaning is used above. Then, is it true that a category $C$ has local initial objects if and only if $C$ has a coreflective subcategory that is a groupoid? For the "only if" direction, let $D$ be the full subcategory of objects $X$ of $C$ for which the slice category $C/X$ has a zero object (note that $(X, \mathrm{id}_X)$ is always terminal, so it also needs to be initial for it to be a zero object). Then, for any object $X$ of $C$ , the initial object of $C/X$ should give a coreflection of $X$ in $D$ . Also, every morphism in $D$ should be an isomorphism (making $D$ a subgroupoid of $C$ ). Conversely, for the "if" direction, let $D$ be a coreflective subgroupoid of $C$ . Then, for any object $X$ of $C$ , the coreflection of $X$ in $D$ should give an initial object of $C/X$ . Is the above correct?

title: Formalizing the notion of gluing in topology
body: I am trying to completly formalise the intuitive idea of Gluing in topology. To give some context to this question, let me give an example of constructing the cylinder out of a square. Constructing the cylinder out of quotient Consider the rectangle $[0,1]^2$ , we formalise gluing the left and right edge as quotienting the set by the minimal equivalence relation generated out of the relation $(0,t) \sim (0,1),\forall t \in I $ , then the resulting space $ [0,1]^2/\sim$ is the cylinder. Constructing the cylinder out of the subspace topology Consider the set $S^1 \times [0,1]$ , we give it the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R^3}$ . Discussion As seen in the above, on an intuitive level, it is pretty easy to see that cylinder should be the same whether it is constructed out of a quotient, or constructed out of the interval which itself has the subspace topology. I have a feeling that if we quotient out any set $\mathbb{R^d}$ and give the quotiented set the quotient of the subspace topology, then that be neccesarily homemorphic to some subset $\mathbb{R^n}$ with subspace topology. (A) Now, do note that once we do the quotient of a set which is a subset of a bigger set, the resulting set is a set of equivalence classes, hence that is no longer a subset of the originally said bigger set. I believe that the subset of $\mathbb{R^n}$ that our quotient is homemorphic too should be the one seen as the result of the gluing action (its should be pretty clear that when we the ends of a paper together in 3D space, we get again something that gets again an induced sense of nearness i.e: topology from the ambient space that it exists in). title: Counting f-invariant subspaces over finite fields
body: Riffing off of On the number of $f$ -stable subsets which I very much enjoyed thinking about, let $f : V \to V$ be a linear map on an $n$ -dimensional vector space over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and define $I(f) = \{ W \subseteq V : f(W) \subseteq W \}$ to be the number of $f$ -invariant subspaces of $W$ . What can we say about the number $I(f)$ ? In addition to considering the question for a fixed value of $f$ , it's also interesting to consider two ways $f$ can vary in families: first, given $f$ defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$ we can extend scalars to define $f/\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ , and consider the family of counts $I(f/\mathbb{F}_{q^k})$ . Second, given $f$ defined over $\mathbb{Z}$ (so acting on a finite free $\mathbb{Z}$ -module) we can extend scalars to define $f/\mathbb{F}_q$ over any finite field, and consider the family of counts $I(f/\mathbb{F}_q)$ . I think taking $f$ -invariant subspaces defines a scheme, specifically a projective subscheme of the disjoint union of the Grassmannians $\text{Gr}_k(V)$ ; if so these point counts are related to the cohomology of this scheme by the Weil conjectures . Anyway, here's what I've got so far. The easiest special case is that $f$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with distinct eigenvalues; in this case an $f$ -invariant subspace is exactly a direct sum of some subset of the $1$ -dimensional eigenspaces, which gives $I(f) = 2^n$ . This is analogous to the case where $f$ is the identity in the set version of the problem. If $f$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{F}_q$ but its eigenspaces have dimensions $m_{\lambda} = \dim V_{\lambda}$ , then an $f$ -invariant subspace is a direct sum of subspaces of the eigenspaces, which gives $$I(f) = \prod_{\lambda} \left( \sum_{k=0}^{m_{\lambda}} {m_{\lambda} \choose k}_q \right)$$ where ${n \choose k}_q$ is the $q$ -binomial coefficients , so the factor in the product corresponding to $\lambda$ counts the total number of subspaces of $V_{\lambda}$ . This is analogous to the case where $f$ is invertible in the set version of the problem. In scheme terms, the scheme of $f$ -invariant subspaces in this case is a product of disjoint unions of Grassmannians. This calculation correctly suggests that we can reduce to considering one (generalized) eigenspace at a time. More precisely, if the characteristic polynomial of $f$ has irreducible factorization $\prod p_i(t)^{m_i}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ , and we write $V$ as a direct sum of the generalized eigenspaces $V_i = \ker(p_i(f)^{m_i})$ and write $f_i : V_i \to V_i$ for the corresponding restrictions, then an $f$ -invariant subspace of $V$ is exactly a tuple of $f_i$ -invariant subspaces of each $V_i$ , so $$I(f) = \prod_i I(f_i).$$ (This follows e.g. from the Chinese remainder theorem applied to the $\mathbb{F}_q[t]/\prod p_i(t)^{m_i}$ -module structure on $V$ where $t$ acts by $f$ .) So we can reduce WLOG to the case that the characteristic polynomial of $f$ is primary (a power of an irreducible). This is analogous to the reduction to the case that $f$ has one connected component in the set case. However, unlike the set case, it is not true that $f$ is multiplicative under direct sums in general, which complicates things. The case that the characteristic polynomial $p(t)$ is irreducible is not so bad; in this case $\mathbb{F}_q[t]/p(t) \cong \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ is a field so $f$ -invariant subspaces correspond to $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ -subspaces of a $1$ -dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ , of which there are $2$ . So $I(f) = 2$ in this case. The next interesting case after this is the case that the characteristic polynomial has the form $(t - \lambda)^n$ ; since the $f$ -invariant subspaces don't change if we replace $f$ with $f - \lambda$ we can assume WLOG that $\lambda = 0$ , so we can reduce to the case that $f$ is nilpotent. If $f$ has a single Jordan block then $f$ preserves a complete flag of $V$ given by its generalized eigenspaces $\ker(f^k)$ , and these are the only $f$ -invariant subspaces, so $I(f) = n + 1$ in this case. However the case that $f$ has multiple Jordan blocks seems complicated, and I'm not sure how it works in general. Here Jordan chains are analogous to the "trees" in the set version of the problem. There appears to be a version of the third case of the " $I$ -recursion" (see the original linked question) in this case but I'm not sure how complicated it ends up being. The general case of characteristic polynomial $p(t)^m$ ought to be a mix of the previous two cases but I'm also not sure how it works in general. Also I have not thought much about what happens if $f$ varies in families as described above. Also there is another variant of this question we could ask where we count subgroups of finite abelian groups (this amounts to replacing the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_q[t]$ by $\mathbb{Z}$ ), which surely must be known and very classical.

title: Show that the ring of germs at 0 is local
body: I have been posed the following problem: Prove that $C_0$ (which is the ring of germs of continuous functions at $0$ ) is a local ring, with maximal ideal $M$ consisting of the germs of functions that vanish at 0. I have shown that $M$ is maximal in $C_0$ , however to prove locality I have: Let $P$ be an ideal in $C_0$ such that it is not $M$ and there exists a surjective homomorphism $\phi: C_0 \to ℝ$ given by $\phi([f]) = f(0)$ . Then, $P$ is maximal in $C_0$ iff $C_0/P$ is isomorphic to ℝ. We see that ℝ is isomorphic to $C_0/P$ only if $\ker(\phi) = P$ . Since $\ker(\phi)$ is precisely $M$ , $P$ must be $M$ . Therefore, the only maximal ideal in $C_0$ is $M$ and $C_0$ is a local ring. My mentor says my solution is incorrect since I did not use the definition of $C_0$ as a ring of germs , could anyone please clarify what is meant by this?

title: No simple group of order 756 : Burnside's proof
body: I'm interested in a proof of the non-simplicity of groups of order 756. W.R. Scott, Group Theory, p. 392, exerc. 13.4.9, gives it as an easy exercise, but depending on rather advanced results. I have a proof using classical methods (merging theorem, Sylow theorems, Burnside's transfer theorem) and also a theorem of Frobenius of which a particular case says that if $G$ is a finite group, if $d$ is a natural divisor of $|G|$ , then the number of elements $x$ of $G$ such that $x^{d} = 1$ is divisible by $d$ . (There is an English translation of Frobenius's paper by R. Andreev here : https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.08813 ) Unfortunately, my proof is very long. Burnside gave a short proof in 1895 (Collected Papers, vol. I, p. 598-599 of the volume). He assumes that there exists a simple group $G$ of order 756 and here is the beginning of his proof (note that the subgroups of order 27 of $G$ are the Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ ) : "If simple, the group must contain $3^{3}.7$ operations [= elements] of even order and $6.36$ operations of order $7$ , leaving $350$ operations whose orders are powers of $3$ . [Today, we would say : $351$ $3$ -elements.] There are $28$ sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ , and, if any of these have a common sub-group of order $3^{2}$ , the group is certainly composite [= not simple]." So far, no problem. (If anybody is interested, I can explain the details.) But then, Burnside says: "The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set." Since, as noted, the intersection of two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ always has order $1$ or $3$ , this amounts to say that the subgroups of order $3$ of $G$ of the form $P \cap Q$ , with $P$ and $Q$ two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ , are all conjugate in $G$ . (In any case, I understand it in this manner.) But how can we prove that ? Of course, it would be true if the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $3$ -subgroups was 2-transitive. (And in this case, two different Sylow $3$ -subgroups of $G$ should always have an intersection of order $3$ , since it is easy to prove that if all Sylow 3-subgroups of $G$ intersected pairwise trivially, the group should have more than $756$ elements.) But is it the case that the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $3$ -subgroups is 2-transitive? As a sufficient condition for the conjugation action of a finite group $G$ on the set of its Sylow $p$ -subgroups to be 2-transitive, I only find this (I can give a proof if anybody is interested :) Theorem . Let $G$ be a finite group, let $p$ be a prime divisor of $\vert G \vert$ , let $p^{m}$ denote the greatest power of $p$ dividing $\vert G \vert$ . Assume that 1° $G$ has several Sylow $p$ -subgroups; 2° $a$ is a natural number < $m-1$ such that the intersection of two different Sylow $p$ -subgroups of $G$ is always of order $\leq p^{a}$ ; (we can take $a$ such that $p^{a}$ is the greatest possible order of $P \cap Q$ , with $P$ and $Q$ two different Sylow $p$ -subgroups of $G$ ) 3° for the same $a$ , we have $\vert Syl_{p}(G)\vert < 2 p^{m-a}$ . Then the conjugation action of $G$ on the set of its Sylow $p$ -subgroups is 2-transitive. But, in Burnside's proof, we have $\vert Syl_{3} (G) \vert = 28$ , $m = 3$ and the least possible value we can take for $a$ is $1$ , not $0$ (as already said, it is easy to see that the $3$ -Sylow subgroups of $G$ cannot intersect all pairwise trivially), so condition 3° is not satisfied. Thus my question is : how can we prove Burnside's assertion : "The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set" ? Thanks in advance. $ \mathbf{Edit}$ (July 5, 2024) Thanks to Derek Holt for his clear explanation. I think this explanation enables us to briefly finish the proof. Let $G$ be, by contradiction, a simple group of order $756$ . Let us say that a subroup $R$ of order $3$ of $G$ is multiplist if it is contained in more than one Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ and let us say that it is unicist in the other case. Similarly, let us say that an element of order $3$ of $G$ is multiplist if it is contained in more than one Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ and let us say that it is unicist in the other case. From Derek Holt's explanation, it results that if $R$ is a multiplist subgroup of order $3$ of $G$ , then $\vert C_{G}(R) \vert = 36$ . Since every proper subgroup of $G$ has order $\leq 36$ , it follows that $\vert N_{G}(R) \vert = 36$ . As stated by Burnside and explained by Derek Holt, all multiplist subgroups of order 3 of $G$ form a conjugacy class, so they are in number $756/36 = 21$ . Thus the multiplist elements of order $3$ of $G$ are in number $42$ . By definition, two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ never have a common unicist element of order $3$ . Moreover, since all Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ are conjugate, they all have the same number of unicist elements of order $3$ . Thus (since, as noted by Burnside, $G$ has exactly $28$ Sylow $3$ -subroups) the number of unicist elements of order $3$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (3)$ and thus by $8$ . As noted by Burnside, two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ never have a common subgroup of order $9$ and thus never have a common element of order $9$ . In the same manner as precedingly, we conclude that the number of elements of order $9$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (9)$ and thus by $8$ . From the fact that every Sylow $3$ -subroup of $G$ is its own normalizer in $G$ and from Burnside's transfer theorem, we could conclude that the Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ are not abelian and thus not cyclic, so $G$ has no element of order $27$ , but without using Burnside's transfer theorem, we can say that clearly no element of order $27$ can be in two distinct Sylow $3$ -subroups of $G$ , so, as above, the number of elements of order $27$ in $G$ is divisible by $28 \times \varphi (27)$ and thus by $8$ . From what precedes, the $3$ -elements of $G$ different from $1$ are in number congruent to $2$ modulo $8$ . But Burnside has shown that the $3$ -elements of $G$ different from $1$ are in number $350$ , not congruent to $2$ modulo $8$ , so we have done. Here is Burnside's complete proof : "If simple, the group must contain $3^{3}.7$ operations [= elements] of even order and $6.36$ operations of order $7$ , leaving $350$ operations whose orders are powers of $3$ . [Today, we would say : $351$ $3$ -elements.] There are $28$ sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ , and, if any of these have a common sub-group of order $3^{2}$ , the group is certainly composite [= not simple]. The sub-groups of order 3 which are common to two sub-groups of order $3^{3}$ form a single conjugate set; and when the group is expressed in $28$ symbols a simple calculation will show that each sub-group of order $3^{3}$ must contain $8$ operations keeping $1$ symbol unchanged and $18$ keeping $4$ symbols unchanged. There are therefore $63$ sub-groups of order $3$ which occur in more than one sub-group of order $3^{3}$ . On the other hand, such a sub-group of order $3$ must (Note VI) be permutable in a sub-group of order $2^{2} /dot 3^{3}$ at least; and must therefore be one of a set of $21$ conjugate sub-groups at most. The supposition that the group is simple thus leads to a contradiction." I don't understand the part of the proof beginning with "and when the group is expressed in $28$ symbols...". Isn't my reasoning sufficient and simpler?

title: A.s. Convergence implies subsequential Complete convergence?
body: The question tries to understand how much stronger is complete convergence as opposed to almost sure convergence. If results that highlight this relationship come to your mind, feel free to share. My question is whether $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$ implies that for a subsequence $X_{n_K}$ we have that $\sum \mathbb{P}(|X_{n_m} -X|<2^{-m}) < \infty$ , subsequential complete convergence that is (we have here chosen $\varepsilon_m = 2^{-m}$ but any other choice would have been fine as long as $\varepsilon_m \to 0$ ). My reasoning was to use the $\sup$ characterization of a.s. convergence (that is: we have a.s. convergence iff $\mathbb{P}(\sup_n |X_n -X| > 2^{-m}) \to 0$ for all m) to elect an index subsequence $(n_m)$ that satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\sup_n |X_{n_m} -X| > 2^{-m}) < 2^{-m}$ , thus yielding the convergence of the above series. Does that seem reasonable? Do you happen to know more insightful results? Thank you.

title: What is the 2nd most likely value of a Random Walk after time=t?
body: Here is a math problem I was thought of the other day involving Random Walks: Let $X_t$ , $t \in \{0, 1, 2, ..., n\}$ , be a (discrete time) stochastic process where $$X_t \in \{-1, +1\}$$ $$P(X_t = +1) = P(X_t = -1) = 0.5$$ . Let $Z_t$ as the position of $X_t$ at each turn $t$ : $$Z_t = \sum_{i=0}^{t} X_i$$ Using the standard properties of a Random Walk, we know that the position of this process at any given time is Normally Distributed. Using this property, we should be able to find out the mean position and variance after any time $t$ . Here is my question: Suppose at $t=0$ , the process starts at position $0$ .Let's say that we let this process run for $t=15$ steps. In this situation: What is the most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? What is the second most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? What is the third most likely position this process will be after 15 steps? etc. On some level, the answer is somewhat obvious. The distribution of possible positions at time $t$ will begin to resemble a Gaussian Distribution (i.e. Bell Curve) as $t$ increases in size. Therefore, the mean value should be the most frequent - and positions closer to the mean value should relatively more frequent compared to positions farther away from the mean value. However, I would like to try and answer this question more mathematically to determine the exact probability that the process occupies any given position after a certain amount of time. To answer this question, I thought that we can start by enumerating the sample space. After $t$ steps, how many unique values could the process have? I thought about this and naively thought that it can have (- $t$ , $t$ ) number of positions. E.g. if $t$ = 15, then : -15 if 15 consecutive -1 , +15 if 15 consecutive +1 ... and everything else in between. But I am not sure if this logic is correct (e.g. need to account for odd valued $t$ vs even valued $t$ ). However, I am not sure if there is some mathematical function (e.g. combinatorial, probability generator function) which can be used to determine the number of ways a certain position can be reached. If this was possible, then I would be able to find all possible ways to end up with all possible positions, and then rank each one in terms of frequency. Can someone please suggest how to work on this problem? Note: Currently, I am using a computer simulation (in R) to experiment with this problem and enumerate all possible paths and frequencies. For example, here are all the probabilities of all possible paths after 15 turns (I have posted the code in case anyone wants to play with this): library(dplyr) generate_all_paths <- function(num_turns) { if (num_turns == 0) { return(list(c())) } else { paths_plus <- generate_all_paths(num_turns - 1) paths_minus <- generate_all_paths(num_turns - 1) paths_plus <- lapply(paths_plus, c, 1) paths_minus <- lapply(paths_minus, c, -1) return(c(paths_plus, paths_minus)) } } paths <- generate_all_paths(15) df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(paths, function(x) { c(x, rep(NA, max(lengths(paths)) - length(x))) })) df <- as.data.frame(df, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) df$final_score <- rowSums(df, na.rm = TRUE) df <- df %>% group_by(final_score) %>% summarise(count = n()) %>% mutate(probability = count / sum(count)) df Now we can see the frequencies and probabilities of all possible paths for a particular process: final_score count probability 1 -15 1 0.0000305 2 -13 15 0.000458 3 -11 105 0.00320 4 -9 455 0.0139 5 -7 1365 0.0417 6 -5 3003 0.0916 7 -3 5005 0.153 8 -1 6435 0.196 9 1 6435 0.196 10 3 5005 0.153 11 5 3003 0.0916 12 7 1365 0.0417 13 9 455 0.0139 14 11 105 0.00320 15 13 15 0.000458 16 15 1 0.0000305

title: What is this Tensor operation?
body: I am trying to identify an operation that takes two matrices of dimensions $n^2$ and output a matrix of dimensions $n^2$ . Every element in the output matrix incorporates all elements from the input matrices. All possible multiplication pairs from elements of the input matrices appear only once throughout the output matrix. So individual output elements have all distinct pairs. Here is an example given the matrices: $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} a_{11} &a_{12} \\ a_{21} &a_{22} \end{array}\right] \;\; , \;\; B = \left[\begin{array}{cc} b_{11} &b_{12} \\ b_{21} &b_{22} \end{array}\right]$$ What is the operation that produce: $$operation(A,B) = \left[\begin{array} \\ a_{11}b_{11}+a_{12}b_{21}+a_{22}b_{12}+a_{21}b_{22} & a_{11}b_{12}+a_{12}b_{22}+a_{22}b_{11}+a_{21}b_{21} \\ a_{21}b_{11}+a_{22}b_{21}+a_{12}b_{12}+a_{11}b_{22} & a_{21}b_{12}+a_{22}b_{22}+a_{12}b_{11}+a_{11}b_{21} \end{array}\right]$$ I find out that it is equivalent to these matrix multiplications; $$operation(A,B) = AB + C_{up} A C_{up} C_{left} B$$ Where $C_{up}$ is a up Cyclic permutation and $C_{left}$ a left one. The second term is basically the following matrix multiplication: $$\left[\begin{matrix} a_{21} & a_{22} \\ a_{11} & a_{12} \end{matrix}\right]\left[\begin{matrix} b_{22} & b_{21} \\ b_{12} & b_{11} \end{matrix}\right]$$ If the matrices are 3x3 instead of 2x2, the result become: $$operation(A,B) = AB + C_{up}A C_{up} C_{left} B + C_{down} A C_{down} C_{right} B$$ Does it relate to a standard tensor operation?

title: Using the theory of simplicial complex to construct a deformation retraction
body: Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $Y$ the normal complex analytic space. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a proper surjective holomorphic map with connected fibers. In a paper, the author told us that, for any point $y\in Y$ , by the Lojaziewic's triangulation theorem, we can choose an open Stein neighborhood $U$ such that there is a deformation retraction $f^{-1}(U)\to X_y:=f^{-1}(y)$ . Question: Why can we choose such $U$ (or how to choose such $U$ )? Clues: 1, The triangulation theorem appears to be as follows: let $X$ be a complex space and $A$ an analytic subset of $X$ . Then there exists a triangulation of $|X|$ in which $A$ appears as the support of a sub-complex. In particular, there exists an open neighbourhood $E$ of $A$ such that $E$ and $\bar{E}$ can be retracted onto $A$ . 2, Consequently, our above question may be reduced to be a purely algebraically-topologically question: how to use the theory of simplicial complex to find such $U$ satisfying that there is a deformation retraction $f^{-1}(U)\to X_y$ ? P.S. Note that when $Y$ is the unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ , In page 101 of the book: 1984, Barth, Peters, Van de Ven, Compact Complex Surfaces, the authors told us that there is a deformation retraction $X\to X_0$ ( However, the method there does not seem to be applicable here .). For more details, see the post Using morse theory to construct a deformation retraction

title: Are these Cayley graphs strongly connected?
body: My Background: I have no formal training in graph theory. I'm just a group theory PhD student. He mentioned something about my research from a graph theoretical perspective. It seemed like a known thing, so I will ask about it here. The Question: Is the (directed) Cayley graph $\operatorname{Cay}(G,T)$ of $G=\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$ with respect to $T$ strongly connected, where $$T=\{g^{-1}sg, g^{-1}s^{-1}g\mid s\in S, g\in G\}$$ for arbitrary, normally generating $S\subseteq G$ , i.e. , $G=\operatorname{ncl}_G(S)$ ? The Details: A graph is strongly connected if for any vertices $x,y$ , there exists a path from $x$ to $y$ and vice versa. Context: Since . . . This is probably known already. I have very little experience with graph theory. It would greatly inform my research. I am unlikely to be able to prove it myself. . . . I would massively appreciate a proof (or counterexample) aimed at an advanced undergraduate level. Thoughts: I think it might have something to do with $T$ being closed under inverses.

title: Kahler differentials and etale fundamental group
body: In Algebraic geometry we can define two notions that generalize tools from topology/differential geometry: the etale fundamental group and the module/sheaf of Kähler differentials. In the complex setting (ie when dealing with an affine or projective smooth complex manifold $X$ ), we can assume both points of view and we can also introduce the integral of a 1-form, say $\omega$ , along a loop $\gamma$ . If $\omega$ is closed we have homotopy invariance of the integral and, thanks to Stokes theorem, we can define a map $\int:\pi_1(X,x)×H^1_{dR}(X,\mathbb{C})\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with nice properties. Of course, to be precise, integration is not defined over non-smooth submanifolds in general, but we can take the homology class of $\gamma$ , and it is a well known fact that in that setting the construction works. So here's the question: does this construction of a pairing in any way generalizes when we consider $X$ as a scheme, replacing the fundamental group with its étale counterpart and holomorphic differentials with algebraic ones? And if that is possible does this works even for more general schemes?

My attempt on the problem is like so: If the median is $60$ , then the sum of the $180$ th and the $181$ st should be $120$ - so that the average between them (since we have an even number of students) is $60$ . Let $i$ denote the grade student $180$ got, $20\leq i\leq 60$ (lower than 20 would cause the $181st$ have grade above $100$ , and higher than $60$ would cause $181$ st have grade below $180$ th. So the $181$ th has grade $120 - i$ . Now let's count the historgrams for the $179$ students who got less than or equal to $i$ (between $0-i$ inclusive): it's a choice with repetitions and without regard to the order at which we choose, so according to the stars and bars result: $${179 + i + 1 - 1\choose 179}={179 + i\choose 179}$$ And let's to the same thing for student who go between $120-i$ and $100$ inclusive: $${179 + (100 - (120 - i) + 1) - 1\choose 179}={159 + i\choose 179}$$ Multiplying both results since they come one after the other and summing it all up, we end up with: $$\sum_{i=20}^{60}{179 + i\choose 179}{159 + i\choose 179}$$ Now, as I asked at the beggining of the question, I would like to know if there is a solution not using sums, but a closed a formula. title: Improving Ellipsoid Theorem $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot n \mathcal{E}$
body: Setting: Definition (ellipsoid): An ellipsoid is $\mathcal{E} := \{y \in \mathbb{R}^n : ||A^{-1}(y-t)|| \leq 1\}$ , i.e images under a given $A$ of full rank of the unit closed ball of $\mathbb{R}^n$ . Definition (convex body): A convex body is a convex compact, with nonempty interior part subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ . Definition (centrally symmetric): $K$ is centrally symmetric if when $x \in K$ then $-x \in K$ I have a proof of the following Theorem: Theorem: For all convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ exists $\mathcal{E}$ centered in $0$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot n \mathcal{E}$ . where $c$ is a constant independent from $n$ , $c > 130$ . Goal: What I'd like to construct is a proof for Theorem: For all centrally symmetric convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ exists $\mathcal{E}$ centered in $0$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $t+\mathcal{E} \subseteq K \subset t + c\cdot \sqrt{n} \mathcal{E}$ . Outline of the proof: I want to modify the proof of the previous theorem, essentially the idea of the proof is to argue by contradiction, wlog using the unit ball. So we find a point $z \in K$ with norm $cn$ by convexity of $K$ , which, up to rotation can be brought onto the $e_1$ direction. Now the idea is to look at the convex hull of $B(0,1) \cup \{cn e_1\}$ and argument to find an ellipsoid inside $K$ with volume greater of the unit ball $V_n$ , ending the proof. The proof is constructive i.e $$\mathcal{E'} := x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\alpha^2_i}(x_i-t_i)^2 \leq 1$$ , where $t = e_1, \alpha_1 = 2,\alpha_i = \sqrt{\frac{n}{n+(1/10)}}$ for $i\geq 2$ . In particular $vol(\mathcal{E'}) > V_n$ if and only if $2\cdot(\frac{n}{n+\frac{1}{10}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}} > 1$ which is (incredibly) true because of $$ 2\cdot(\frac{n}{n+\frac{1}{10}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}} \geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{10n}}})^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{10n}}}) \geq 2\cdot(\frac{1}{e^{\frac{1}{20}}}) > 1$$ This is important since if we show that $\mathcal{E'} \subset$ convex hull of $B(0,1) \cup \{cn e_1\}$ we are done. In order to do this, we parametrize the line segment between $cn \cdot e_1$ and a vector $y$ such that $||y|| = 1$ with $y_1 = 0$ , up to rotations we can take $e_2$ and show that for the points of the line segment $x_{\lambda} = \lambda e_2 + (1-\lambda)cn e_1$ it holds that $$\sum\limits_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\alpha^2_i}(x_{\lambda}-t)_i^2 > 1$$ for $\lambda \in [0,1]$ . This is true because if $\lambda \geq 1 - \frac{1}{30n}$ then $(1+\frac{1}{10n})(1-\frac{1}{30n})^2 > 1$ . While for $0 \leq \lambda < 1 - \frac{1}{30n}$ then $\frac{1}{4}((1-\lambda)cn - 1)^2 \geq \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{30n}cn-1)^2 > 1$ for $c$ large enough $\Box$ . At this point, I thought take replacing $\alpha_i$ by putting simply $\sqrt{n}$ would have worked (hear the "ice cream" convex hull has two cones so that we can replace t=0, centering it in the origin), and indeed it does with different inequalities and constants if it wasn't that in showing $vol(\mathcal{E'}) > V_n$ I made a mistake not realizing that the basis of the exponential is smaller than $1$ . I know this theorem holds with $C =1$ , for example, a reference can be found in "A course in Convexity" by Barvinok , but I think the proof is unnecessarily complicated since here we don't require that $C=1$ . Do you have an idea how to adjust the argument? Any help would be appreciated.

title: Truncated Tarski's theorem without axiom of choice
body: I read there that the fact about equivalence of $A$ and $A^2$ for any infinite set $A$ and the axiom of choice are equivalent. But what if we prove it only for sets that have cardinality of $\aleph_n, n \in \mathbb{N}\cup\lbrace 0 \rbrace$ . Let's prove it with mathematical induction. For $n = 0$ it's evident, we can use the same proof that was used for the countability of $\mathbb{Q}$ . Suppose that it's true for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . Let's prove it for $n + 1$ . Consider a set $A$ with cardinality of $\aleph_{n + 1}$ . Then there exists a set $B$ with cardinality of $\aleph_n$ which powerset is equivalent to $A$ : $A \sim 2^B$ . Then every element of $A$ corresponds to a subset of $B$ . We can construct an injection between $(2^B)^2$ and $2^B$ . First, we construct an injection between $(2^B)^2$ and $2^{B^2}$ : $f(S_1, S_2) = S_1 \times S_2$ . Further we can construct an injection between $2^{B^2}$ and $2^B$ by using, as we assume, existing injection between $B^2$ and $B$ . Also we can easily can construct an injection between $2^B$ and $(2^B)^2$ : $f(S) = (S, S)$ . Then by the Cantor-Bernstein theorem we have that $A \sim 2^B \sim (2^B)^2 \sim A^2$ As far as I'm concerned, that proof doesn't use the axiom of choice. But it doesn't work for such cardinals as $\aleph_\omega, \aleph_{\omega + 1}$ and so on, because there we should use transfinite induction which uses the axiom of choice. Did I get it right?

title: Images of structure preserving maps are structures?
body: Context : I have been working with (mostly concrete) categories like Sets, Groups, Rings, Vect $_k$ , Ab, $R$ -Mod, Top, Diff and so on. As I understand it, images of group maps are subgroups of their co-domain groups. Hence images of group maps are groups. Same for other “algebraic categories” in my list. However, this seems to break down for Top and Diff (the category of smooth manifolds and smooth maps between them). In Top I need to specify a topology on the image of the continuous map and it somehow “does not come automatically with a topology” unlike group images which come with a group structure ie the the group structure inherited from the co-domain group. In fact one can show that if the underlying set of the image of a group map has a group structure, then it is indeed this subgroup structure inherited from the co-domain group. Moreover, in Top it may seem somewhat canonical to equip the image with the subspace topology of the co-domain space. At least, it is the coarsest topology that makes the inclusion of the image of a continuous map into its image continuous. However, unlike in Groups, this is not the only structure on the image that makes the inclusion continuous. I feel like, things get even worse in Diff , where it seems to be the case that except when the smooth maps are also smooth embeddings or injective smooth immersions, there is no canonical choice of topology and smooth structure for the image of a smooth map. For instance the figure “8” curve is not even a manifold wrt subspace topology even though it is the image of a smooth map (its not smoothly embedded but it is smoothly immersed in the plane. Question : Why is this happening? More precisely, why is it that in categories of groups and rings, images of structure preserving maps are sets with those structures, but NOT in Top or Diff ? Is there a category theory explanation for this? One possible argument I could expect is that smooth structure and indeed topology are structures that we need add on to sets. But I would really like to see some elaboration on this, if possible.

title: Help with the proof of this statement
body: Let $ f : [a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ be a bounded function. Then for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that for any partition $D$ of the interval $[a, b]$ with norm $\nu(D)$ smaller than $\delta$ , the following holds: $$ \left| U(f, D) - \int_a^b \overline{f}(x) \, dx \right| < \epsilon. $$ The upper Riemann integral is the infimum over all partitions of the upper sum. The left side is an upper sum with respect to partition $D$ . The infimum on all the sums is given by: $\inf_{D} U(f, D)$ The right side is the upper integral, which is the infimum over all partitions of the upper sum: $\overline{\int_a^b} f(x) \, dx = \inf_{D} U(f, D)$ The way I would do it is to get an arbitrary upper sum within $\epsilon/2$ of the integral.

title: If every sequence of Riemann sums of a function converges, is the function integrable?
